subject: Kemi
title: Chemical bonds and ions
sourceSummary: Why atoms bind together into compounds, the difference between ionic bonding and covalent bonding, how salts are built from ions in crystals, and common ions and their charges.

questions.prompt: Why do atoms bind together into compounds?
questions.opener: Think about what the noble gases have that makes them so stable, and what other atoms lack.
choices: Because they are drawn to each other by magnetism
Because they want to become heavier
Because they strive for a full outer electron shell, which gives a more stable state
Because all atoms must sit in pairs
questions.explanation: Atoms bind together to achieve a full outer electron shell, in other words the same stable electron arrangement that the noble gases have. This is about the electrons in the outer shell, not magnetism — and the number of atoms in a compound can vary, it doesn't have to be two.

questions.opener: The name gives away that ions are involved — think about what ions have that draws them to each other.
choices: Electrical attraction between positive and negative ions, formed when one atom has given up electrons to another
Two atoms sharing a pair of electrons
A bond in which two atomic nuclei fuse into one
A bond that can only exist between two metals
questions.explanation: In ionic bonding, electrons have moved completely from one atom to another, so that positive and negative ions form and are drawn to each other by electrical attraction. Sharing a pair of electrons is instead a covalent bond, and ionic bonding typically arises between a metal and a non-metal — not between two metals.

questions.prompt: What characterises a covalent bond (molecular bond)?
questions.opener: Here no electrons move all the way across — instead they are used jointly.
choices: That one atom takes over all the electrons from the other atom
That two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons
That ions swap places with each other in a crystal
That a metal gives up electrons to a non-metal
questions.explanation: In a covalent bond, two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, and in this way both get a full outer shell — this is how H2O and O2 are held together, for example. Electrons moving completely from a metal to a non-metal is instead ionic bonding.

questions.prompt: Which statement about table salt, NaCl, is correct?
questions.opener: Think about whether salt consists of separate molecules or of some other pattern.
choices: It consists of separate NaCl molecules that sit together in pairs
It contains only sodium atoms
It never conducts electricity, not even when dissolved in water
It is an ionic compound of sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl−) arranged in a crystal lattice
questions.explanation: Table salt is an ionic compound in which Na+ and Cl− are packed regularly in a crystal lattice — the formula NaCl shows the ratio 1:1, not a single molecule. If the salt is dissolved in water, the ions are freed and can move, and then the solution conducts electricity.

questions.prompt: Magnesium is in group 2 of the periodic table. Which ion does a magnesium atom form?
questions.opener: The group number 2 tells you how many valence electrons the atom has to get rid of.
choices: Mg−
Mg+
Mg2+
Mg2−
questions.explanation: Magnesium has two valence electrons and gives up both to get a full outer shell, which gives the ion Mg2+ with a charge of 2+. Metals give up electrons and become positive ions, so a negative magnesium ion is not formed.

questions.prompt: An oxygen atom has six valence electrons. Which ion does it form?
questions.opener: Work out how many electrons are missing for the shell to become full with eight.
choices: O+
O−
questions.explanation: Oxygen is missing two electrons to reach eight in the outer shell, so the atom takes up two electrons and becomes the oxide ion O2− with a charge of 2−. Taking up electrons gives a negative charge, so a positive oxygen ion is not formed, and O− has only taken up one of the two electrons.

questions.prompt: Magnesium (group 2) reacts with chlorine (group 17). Show which ions are formed and work out the formula of the ionic compound.
questions.opener: Determine the charge on each ion first, then work out how many of each are needed for the charges to cancel out.
questions.answer: Magnesium gives up two electrons and forms Mg2+, while each chlorine atom takes up one electron and forms Cl−. Two chloride ions are needed per magnesium ion for the charges to cancel out, so the formula is MgCl2 (magnesium chloride).
steps: Magnesium is in group 2 and has two valence electrons that the metal readily gives up.
When both electrons are given up, the ion Mg2+ is formed.
Chlorine is in group 17 and has seven valence electrons — each chlorine atom takes up one electron and forms Cl−.
The ionic compound must be uncharged overall, so the charge 2+ must be balanced by two ions with a charge of 1−.
This gives the ratio one Mg2+ to two Cl−, in other words the formula MgCl2, magnesium chloride.

questions.prompt: Summarise chemical bonds, ions and ionic compounds.
questions.opener: Start with the driving force behind all bonds, then take the two bond types and finish with common ions.
questions.answer: Driving force: atoms bind together to get a full outer electron shell, like the noble gases · Ionic bonding: electrons move completely across, positive and negative ions are drawn to each other, occurs between a metal and a non-metal · Ionic compound (salt): ions packed in a crystal lattice, the formula shows the ratio between the ions, e.g. NaCl · Salt dissolved in water: the ions are freed and the solution conducts electricity · Covalent bonding (molecular bond): two non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons, forming molecules such as H2, O2, H2O and CO2 · Positive ions (metals give up electrons): Na+, K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Al3+ · Negative ions (non-metals take up electrons): Cl−, O2−, S2− · Compound ions: OH− (hydroxide ion), NO3− (nitrate ion), SO42− (sulfate ion), CO32− (carbonate ion) · Rule for formulas: the charges must cancel out, e.g. Mg2+ + 2 Cl− → MgCl2 and Ca2+ + O2− → CaO · Ionic compounds have high melting points, molecular compounds usually low ones.

questions.prompt: What electron configuration do atoms aim for when they form bonds?
questions.opener: Think about which group of elements is already stable without needing to bond.
choices: A completely empty outer shell
The same stable configuration as the noble gases (a full outer shell)
As many electrons as possible regardless of shell
No particular configuration
questions.explanation: Atoms aim for a full outer electron shell, just like the noble gases already have naturally. A completely empty outer shell is not the goal — it's how full the shell is that determines stability.

questions.prompt: Between which types of substances does ionic bonding usually occur?
questions.opener: Think about which kind of atom readily gives up electrons and which readily takes them up.
choices: Between two non-metals
Between a metal and a non-metal
Between two noble gases
Only within the same element
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding typically occurs between a metal, which readily gives up electrons, and a non-metal, which readily takes them up. Two non-metals instead usually share electrons through covalent bonding.

questions.prompt: Which of these substances is held together by covalent bonding?
questions.opener: Think about which substance is made up entirely of non-metal atoms.
choices: NaCl (table salt)
MgO (magnesium oxide)
H2O (water)
CaCl2 (calcium chloride)
questions.explanation: Water (H2O) consists of hydrogen and oxygen, two non-metals that share electron pairs through covalent bonding. NaCl, MgO and CaCl2 are instead ionic compounds between a metal and a non-metal.

questions.prompt: What happens to the ions in a salt when it dissolves in water?
questions.opener: Think about why salt water conducts electricity but plain water barely does.
choices: They are destroyed completely
They are freed and can move around, which lets the solution conduct electricity
They fuse together into a single ion
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: When the salt dissolves, the ions are freed from the crystal lattice and can move freely in the water, which lets the solution conduct electricity. In the solid salt, the ions are instead fixed in place and can't carry charge.

questions.prompt: Calcium is in group 2 of the periodic table. Which ion does a calcium atom form?
questions.opener: The group number tells you how many valence electrons the atom has to get rid of.
choices: Ca−
Ca+
Ca2+
Ca2−
questions.explanation: Calcium has two valence electrons and gives up both to get a full outer shell, forming the ion Ca2+ with a charge of 2+. Metals give up electrons and become positive ions, never negative ones.

questions.prompt: Calcium (group 2) reacts with oxygen (which takes up two electrons to get a full shell). Show which ions form and work out the formula of the ionic compound.
questions.opener: Determine the charge of each ion first, then see how many of each are needed for the charges to cancel out.
questions.answer: Calcium gives up two electrons and forms Ca2+, while each oxygen atom takes up two electrons and forms O2−. The charges 2+ and 2− cancel out exactly one to one, so the formula is CaO (calcium oxide).
steps: Calcium is in group 2 and has two valence electrons that the metal readily gives up.
When both electrons are given up, the ion Ca2+ forms.
Oxygen takes up two electrons to get a full outer shell and forms the ion O2−.
The ionic compound must be uncharged overall, and the charge 2+ is exactly balanced by the charge 2−.
This gives a ratio of one Ca2+ to one O2−, so the formula is CaO, calcium oxide.

questions.prompt: What characterises molecular compounds compared with ionic compounds in terms of melting point?
questions.opener: Think about the difference between melting ice and melting table salt.
choices: Molecular compounds usually have a higher melting point
Molecular compounds usually have a lower melting point
They always have exactly the same melting point
Melting point never depends on bond type
questions.explanation: Molecular compounds usually have considerably lower melting points than ionic compounds, since the forces between molecules are weaker than the electrical attraction in an ionic lattice. Ice, for example, melts at 0°C, while table salt melts above 800°C.
